Five Walton heirs have added $100 billion to their fortunes in 2026, roughly what Oracle's Larry Ellison lost, despite never founding or running a company.

Walmart's stock has climbed 13% this year, outpacing the S&P 500 and dodging the AI sell-off, lifting its market value to $1 trillion.

One could say the Walton family does not deserve to be rich. Among the world's wealthiest people, they are the only ones who did not start or serve as senior management of a company, most of which are in the tech industry. Nevertheless, five of Walmart (NYSE: WMT) founder Sam Walton's children and grandchildren have watched their combined net worth rise by $100 billion so far in 2026, Bloomberg reports. That is about the amount Oracle (NASDAQ: ORCL) founder Larry Ellison has lost in the same period.

Sam Walton started Walmart in 1942, at the age of 44. According to the Fortune 500, it was America's largest company for several years, until it yielded that position to Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN) last year.

Niloo138 / iStock Editorial via Getty Images

Walmart remains a juggernaut. It employs 2.1 million people ("associates" as the company calls them). In the US, the figure is 1.6 million. Its footprint in its home market is 4,600 Walmart stores and 600 Sam's Club locations. Ninety percent of the US population lives within 10 miles of a Sam's Club or Walmart location.

In the most recent quarter, Walmart revenue rose 5.9% to $187.9 billion. Operating income rose 2.9% to $9.4 billion. John Furner, Walmart's President and CEO, said, "Our team delivered another good quarter, and we continue to make steady progress on the long-term value drivers of our business. Our multi-year growth in eCommerce is evidence that customers are choosing Walmart because we deliver price, speed, and convenience
across a broad assortment. At Walmart, they can have it all."

title: AI Stocks Are Falling; Bitcoin Is Holding Ground. Here's What Could Come Next.
detail:
AI Stocks Are Falling; Bitcoin Is Holding Ground. Here's What Could Come Next.
Alex Carchidi, The Motley Fool
Sat, November 7, 2026 at 10:51 AM CST 5 min read
BTC-USD
INTC
NVDA
ORCL
MU
Trade BTC on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

It's been said that bull markets end when good news fails to boost prices, and that bear markets end when bad news fails to send prices lower. On that note, Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC) is 33.7% above its bear market lows in late June. Most of the high-flying artificial intelligence (AI) value-chain stocks, on the other hand -- including Intel, Oracle, Micron Technology, and Sandisk -- are down by between 20% and 62% in the same period.

There are plenty of good reasons for those stocks to be down. Yet aside from emerging factors like questionable future demand for some of the technologies those companies make, all of those players, as well as Bitcoin, have faced a constant onslaught of geopolitical and macroeconomic uncertainty this year. Their diverging prices amid those shared headwinds mean that one thing in particular could be coming next.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.
Bitcoin's floor hasn't collapsed yet

Bitcoin didn't just start shrugging off bad news in the last couple of months. On Sept. 15, the Senate failed to advance the Clarity Act, a bill intended to set rules for crypto market structures. It briefly fell below $75,000 that day, then recovered within weeks.

Then, October saw the Nasdaq Composite index fall more than 5%, as big spenders on AI failed to wow the market with their earnings reports as well as their future projections. Bitcoin dropped 10.3% in the 30-day period ending on Nov. 5, but it largely traded in a range: every daily close was between $76,198 and $84,082, regardless of what was happening in the world. That resilience had to face down a handful of problems that also weighed on tech stocks.

For instance, on Oct. 28, the Federal Reserve voted to hold interest rates steady, and the very next day's hot inflation data caused markets to expect a December hike. Rate hikes tend to be bad for risky assets like AI stocks and cryptocurrencies, as higher rates mean investors can earn a better return on low-risk Treasuries.

Before that, Brent crude oil prices climbed in October as the prospect of continued war with Iran contributed to a highly uncertain environment. Uncertainty tends to weigh on riskier assets, and rising energy costs drive inflation, which might prompt the Federal Reserve to hike interest rates further.

Key Takeaways

Cerebras shares fell 18% in a week as AI stocks sold off on Oracle's $20 billion raise and again after the midterms.

Cerebras made no announcement of its own, and CoreWeave and Oracle fell on the same AI worries.

Analysts expect revenue to more than triple next year, and the stock's forward sales multiple has fallen far from its June peak.

The third-quarter report and the IPO lockup's end come close together, so waiting for the numbers makes more sense.

Cerebras Systems (CBRS:NASDAQ) stock is down 18% in the past week without any news of its own. The AI trade sold off twice, taking CoreWeave (CRWV:NASDAQ) and Oracle (ORCL:NYSE), its newest cloud partner, down too.

Oracle's $20 billion bill landed on its partners

Oracle agreed on Oct. 27 to offer Cerebras's inference on its cloud. Before Monday's open, Oracle filed to raise $20 billion in stock and bonds for its AI buildout. AI infrastructure stocks slid, and Oracle fell 11% over the week. UBS cut its target to $250 from $330 that morning but kept a Buy, so the cut doesn't explain the drop. For now, the deal is more liability than help. It's too new to show up in revenue, yet the stock already trades on how Oracle funds its data centers.

Thursday's rout hit every data-center name

On Thursday, chip and AI stocks sank on fears the Democrats' midterm sweep will tighten AI rules and slow new data centers. The Nasdaq Composite fell 6%, and the Philadelphia chip index 12%. CoreWeave's growth depends on new data centers just as Cerebras's does, and it's down 16% in the past week. It ended June with about $104 billion in revenue backlog. Its next report will show whether that fear reaches customers' orders.

CoreWeave and Nebius plunged about 47% and 45% in a month as rate pressure hit debt-funded AI data center builders.

Microsoft's $19 billion in free cash flow lets it build without borrowing, while Alphabet turned to $29 billion in new bonds.

Fed Chair Kevin Warsh warned "Interest rates get in the cracks," and markets see a 72% chance of another December hike.

Read More: Learn 7 ways to generate income with a $1,000,000+ portfolio (sponsor)

On October 28, Fed Chair Kevin Warsh summed up the AI market's weak spot in six words: "Interest rates get in the cracks." Then he added: "Interest rates affect directly or indirectly almost everything." That includes the AI data center buildout, and a large share of it is paid for with borrowed money.

24/7 Wall St.

In the month ending November 6, CoreWeave (NASDAQ:CRWV) fell 47.54% and Nebius Group (NASDAQ:NBIS) dropped 45.4%. Over the same month, Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) edged up 0.16%. The market now sorts AI companies by one question: who pays for data centers with cash, and who borrows to build them?

Two Rate Squeezes Hitting at Once

The Fed raised its benchmark rate by a quarter point in September and held it at 3.75% to 4.00% in October. As of November 3, CME FedWatch put the odds of another quarter-point hike in December at 72%. Long-term rates are adding a second pressure. The 10-year Treasury yield reached 5.24% on October 9 and still stood at 4.84% on November 5. That same day, the VIX volatility index rose to 28.18, its highest reading since early August.

Borrowers Are Feeling It First

CoreWeave shows the problem most clearly. Its revenue backlog is $104.2 billion, but to deliver it the company plans to spend $35 billion to $39 billion on capital projects this year, and its debt is 8.94 times its equity. Second-quarter interest expense was $640 million, up from $267 million a year earlier. Management expects $860 million to $940 million in the third quarter.

title: CoreWeave’s Bonds Now Yield More Than 16%, Days Before Earnings

CoreWeave’s Bonds Now Yield More Than 16%, Days Before Earnings

Quick Read

CoreWeave's 2032 bond yields over 16% against a 10% coupon, signaling lenders doubt it can keep refinancing before its November 10 earnings.

Microsoft supplied roughly 67% of CoreWeave's 2025 revenue, while it winds down an Oracle rental deal and trims its smaller neocloud suppliers.

Credit stress is rising at NVIDIA and Amazon too, yet levels remain low, so the strain stays concentrated on the weakest borrower.

Read More: Learn 7 ways to generate income with a $1,000,000+ portfolio (sponsor)

On November 6, 2026, the 2032 bond of CoreWeave (NASDAQ:CRWV) traded at a yield above 16%, even though it pays a coupon of only 9.625%. Lenders usually ask for that kind of return only when they doubt a company can keep refinancing.

24/7 Wall St.

The bond move followed a jump in the cost of insuring CoreWeave's debt. A credit default swap works like an insurance policy: the buyer pays an annual premium and collects if the borrower defaults. Five-year protection rose above 1,289 basis points on November 5, which works out to an annual premium of about 12.9% of the debt insured. It then fell about 8% to around 1,155 basis points on November 6.

The stock moved in the opposite direction. Shares fell 9.83% on November 5 to $43.66, then traded at $46.40 late on November 6, up 6.28%. That bounce had no clear link to the bond market.

Third-quarter results are scheduled for November 10 after the close. Right now, bondholders and stock analysts are pricing two very different companies, and that report is the first real test of which group is right.

Why a 16% Yield Raises Borrowing Costs

A bond that yields far more than its coupon trades well below face value, because buyers will hold it only at a discount large enough to lift their return. In mid-October, the $1.25 billion issue traded at 15% and closed at 14.5%. It now yields more than it did then.

Key Takeaways

Bloom Energy fell 12% in the past week as Democrats' midterm sweep sank AI stocks, despite new deals with NTT DATA and California Resources.

Bloom made 97% of its third-quarter revenue in the US, so slower US data-center approvals are the main risk, and Oracle's spending is the thing to watch.

Consensus still puts Bloom's 2028 normalized EPS at more than 10 times its 2025 level, which makes the drop a buying opportunity.

Bloom Energy (BE:NYSE) is down 12% in the past week, though its own news was all good, including a fuel-cell plan with California Resources (CRC:NYSE).

Investors sold on the election anyway, and the customer behind Bloom's biggest order sank with it. Oracle (ORCL:NYSE), which signed a 2.8-gigawatt deal with Bloom, fell 11%.

Bloom's customers kept signing

California Resources said after Monday's close that the two will look at building 1 gigawatt or more of Bloom fuel cells with carbon capture in California. It's non-binding, and we'll learn whether California Resources is paying for it when it sets its 2027 budget early next year. Then on Thursday morning, NTT DATA said it'll deploy 900 megawatts of Bloom's onsite power at data centers worldwide, with shipments starting in 2027.

Investors dumped the whole AI trade

Democrats won control of Congress on Tuesday, and AI stocks sold off on fears the data-center buildout would stall. Bloom has more riding on that than most, since 97% of its third-quarter revenue came from the US. Texas's incoming governor, Gina Hinojosa, has also promised a moratorium on new data-center approvals.

That makes Oracle the customer to watch. It burned $5 billion of free cash flow in the quarter ended Aug. 31 building data centers. Results come in mid-December, and any sign it's slowing that build would put Bloom's biggest order in question.

Snowflake (SNOW) stock gained 56.8% between February 9 and November 6, 2026, while the S&P 500 returned 6.8% over the same dates. The rise was not steady. The stock recorded its two largest one-day gains of that stretch in the sessions immediately following the company's quarterly reports on May 27 and September 2. Those two days alone added more than the whole rise, and the shares have since fallen from a high close of $368.89 on October 9 to $275.88 on November 6. Your view of this move turns on how fast sales are growing and how much more buyers now pay for those sales while Snowflake still loses money. What did Snowflake report just before those two days?

What Snowflake Reported In May And September

On May 27, Snowflake reported product revenue of $1.33 billion for fiscal Q1 2027, up 34% from a year earlier. The shares rose 36.5% the next day, marking the largest one-session gain of the whole rise.

On September 2, the company reported fiscal Q2 2027 product revenue of $1.49 billion, up 37% from a year earlier. Management called it the third straight quarter in which product revenue growth sped up, and the stock added 16.6% the following session.

How Much Of Snowflake's Business Is Growing Faster?

Nearly all of it: product revenue made up 95.5% of Snowflake's sales in fiscal 2026, so faster product growth is, in effect, faster growth for the whole company. Total revenue growth rose in each quarter from 28.7% in fiscal Q3 2026 to 35.1% in fiscal Q2 2027.

Management said on the September 2 call that newer AI products contributed about half of the speed-up in product growth. Management also raised its fiscal 2027 forecast for product revenue to $6.07 billion, which would be 36% growth.

Losses narrowed as well. Snowflake's operating loss equaled 17.0% of revenue in fiscal Q2 2027, compared with 29.7% in fiscal Q2 2026.

Snowflake Still Reports A Net Loss

Snowflake had a net loss of $1.09 billion over the twelve months to July 31, 2026, compared with $1.38 billion a year earlier. It reported a net loss in fiscal Q4 2026, which ended on January 31, 2026, before the rise began, and in both quarters since.

With no profit, Snowflake's price-to-earnings ratio is not meaningful. The stock trades at 17.7 times its sales, compared with 3.1 times for the S&P 500. At the end of March 2026, Snowflake's multiple was 10.4 times sales, so buyers now pay far more for each dollar of sales while the company still reports a loss.
